gap: No result ChatGPT got states that portable projectors lose most of their rated brightness on battery: Projector Reviews measured the Nebula Capsule 3 Laser at 344 ANSI lumens on AC but 126 on battery. XGIMI's 2.5-hour battery claim for the MoGo 4 is for ECO mode, which ProjectorCentral measured at 151–154 ISO lumens against the 450 on the box. Both are about 1/20 of the 3,000 lumens Epson rates for its plug-in CO-FH02.
standout_why: I read the cited beecommercer page (2026-11-14). It lists only rated figures: Capsule 3 Laser '300 ANSI lumens', Epson CO-FH02 '3,000 white ISO / 3,000 color IDMS'. It already separates Epson's white and color ratings, so that part of the normalisation is taken. Its only battery comment is a general line on the BenQ GV50 ('Battery and corrected geometry can reduce usable brightness'). It gives no lumen figure on battery or in ECO for any model. I tried the other cited page, rottenwifi.com, three times and it timed out each time, so I could not check it. ChatGPT's own answer calls the Capsule 3 Laser 'better suited to dark rooms' from its rated 300 lumens. It never says the rating falls further on battery.
decides: It backs ChatGPT's pick of the plug-in Epson CO-FH02 for meeting rooms. It also changes the advice for anyone who chose 'pocket-sized, battery-powered': on battery the Capsule 3 Laser measured 126 ANSI lumens. The MoGo 4's rated 2.5 hours is for ECO mode, measured at about 151–154 ISO lumens, about a third of its 450 rating. So a battery-only presenter needs a dark room and a small image whatever the rated lumens say. If the room has a socket, the plug-in Epson is the pick.
